ukmt-pink-2018-01.title: Use the triangle inequality
ukmt-pink-2018-01.body:
In a triangle each side is shorter than the sum of the other two and longer than their difference. So the third side is less than $5+2=7$ and more than $5-2=3$ cm. The only odd integer strictly between 3 and 7 is 5.

**Answer: (C) 5 cm**

ukmt-pink-2018-11.title: Slide the curved pieces
ukmt-pink-2018-11.body:
Divide the square of side 4 into 16 unit squares. The curved pieces can be slid (as in the official solution) so that the shaded part exactly fills 8 of the unit squares. So the shaded area is 8 and the non-shaded area is $16-8=8$.

**Answer: (C) 8**

ukmt-pink-2018-11.title: Calculate with the semicircles
ukmt-pink-2018-11.body:
Each semicircle has radius 1 (its diameter runs from a vertex to the midpoint of an edge), so its area is $\frac\pi2$. At each corner two semicircles overlap in a lens of area $2\left(\frac\pi4-\frac12\right)=\frac\pi2-1$, and this lens is the white part at the corner.

The shaded region at one corner has area (the two semicircles) minus (twice the lens): $2\times\frac\pi2-2\left(\frac\pi2-1\right)=2$. With four corners the shaded area is $4\times2=8$, so the non-shaded part has area $16-8=8$.

**Answer: (C) 8**

ukmt-pink-2018-21.title: Radius of the circles
ukmt-pink-2018-21.body:
Each circle touches both boundary circles, so its diameter is $9-1=8$ and its radius is 4. Its centre is $1+4=5$ from the centre $O$ of the annulus.

Two neighbouring circles touch when their centres are 8 apart. In the triangle formed by $O$ and two such centres the sides are $5,5,8$, so by the cosine rule the angle $\theta$ at $O$ satisfies $\cos\theta=\frac{25+25-64}{50}=-0.28$, giving $\theta\approx106^\circ$. Each circle therefore uses at least $106^\circ$ of the way round, so at most $\lfloor360/106.3\rfloor=3$ circles fit, and three do fit since $3\times106.3^\circ<360^\circ$.

**Answer: (B) 3**

ukmt-pink-2018-23.title: The numbers repeat every 6 vertices
ukmt-pink-2018-23.body:
Let two adjacent numbers be $a$ and $b$. The next numbers are $b-a$, then $-a$, $-b$, $a-b$, and then $a$, $b$ again. So the pattern repeats every 6 vertices. Since $18=3\times6$ the pattern fits exactly three times round the polygon.

Counting round from $P$ as vertex 0, the vertices marked 20 and 18 are vertices 7 and 11, which are in the same places in the 6-cycle as the neighbours of $P$ (vertices 1 and 17, since $7\equiv1$ and $11\equiv17\pmod 6$). So the neighbours of $P$ hold 20 and 18. Since each number is the sum of its two neighbours, $P=20+18=38$.

**Answer: (B) 38**
